candidates.evidence: match_library top candidate, score 0.88, frequency scale 1.02. All four measured peaks matched within 3 cm-1 (93.79 vs Ag 93.1; 161.27 vs B3g 162.6; 192.85 vs Ag 190.5; 221.44 vs Ag 224.8). No strong reference modes missing. Source: Bagheri and Komsa 2023, Sci. Data 10, 80 (CRD row 4496).

Second match, score 0.71. Four peaks matched but five strong Ag reference modes (122, 155, 184, 203, 209 cm-1) are missing from the spectrum. Not a plausible identity for a layered chalcogenide, so it is rejected.

No SnSe-specific score was returned in the top 5 of match_library, and the skill has no SnSe literature table. Literature in this session: Li et al. 2017 (Nanoscale, doi 10.1039/c7nr05047j) reports strong SnSe Ag modes at 130 and 150 cm-1, and Sriv et al. 2020 (Sci. Rep. 10, 11761, doi 10.1038/s41598-020-68744-2) lists Ag1, Ag2, B3g1, B3g2, Ag3, Ag4 for SnSe1-xSx without numbers in the abstract. The measured spectrum has no line near 130 or 150 cm-1. Confidence is low because the SnSe numeric mode table was not retrieved here.

hint_reasoning: The stated material is SnSe, which is Pnma like SnS. The spectrum has four peaks at 93.8, 161.3, 192.8 and 221.4 cm-1. The top library match is SnS (CRD row 4496), with all four peaks matched at scale 1.02 and no strong missing modes. The literature I could retrieve (Li et al. 2017, doi 10.1039/c7nr05047j) places the strong SnSe Ag modes at 130 and 150 cm-1, and neither has a measured line here. Nearest measured line to the SnSe Ag ~150 is 161.3 cm-1, about 11 cm-1 off. The data therefore do not support SnSe. The most consistent identity is SnS. A SnS-SnSe alloy cannot be excluded from one spectrum, but the Sriv et al. abstract says the low-frequency Ag1 and Ag2 modes of alloys show one-mode behaviour, so an alloy would not explain a 150 to 161 cm-1 shift by itself. The mode-by-mode SnSe numbers were not retrieved from source and should be checked against Sriv et al. 2020 before final sign-off.

limits: The data show four peaks between 60 and 1100 cm-1 at 295 K with 532 nm excitation in backscattering. There is no polarization series, no substrate line and no high-frequency data above 1100 cm-1. Irreps and polarization patterns are not measured here, so pattern is null throughout.
The top library match is SnS, not SnSe. The SnS identification comes from DFT (CRD) frequencies scaled by 1.02, so it is a computed match and not a reference spectrum measured on SnS.

The SnSe numeric mode table was not retrieved from source. The only numbers used for SnSe come from the Li et al. 2017 abstract (130 and 150 cm-1 Ag modes). The Sriv et al. 2020 abstract names the modes without giving positions. A full SnSe comparison needs the table or figure from Sriv et al. 2020, which I could not read because the iopic-bond tool has no VALENCY_BOND_TOKEN here.

The SnS and SnSe Raman mode lists were not compared against each other in a same-setup measurement, so the discrimination rests on the 130 and 150 cm-1 SnSe lines and the CRD match alone. Peak-position differences between SnS and SnSe are typically tens of cm-1 for the main modes, but I did not check that here against a source.

A single spectrum cannot exclude a SnS-SnSe alloy, or a mixed or oxidized sample. The Sriv et al. 2020 abstract reports one-mode behaviour for the low-frequency alloy modes, so an alloy is not an easy fit to a 150 to 161 cm-1 shift alone. Composition would need EDX, XRD or a reference SnSe spectrum taken with the same setup.
The broad 221 cm-1 peak (FWHM 10.7 cm-1, position error 0.7 cm-1) could contain an unresolved second component. It is not resolved at this SNR, so I did not split it.

Laser heating at 532 nm can soften and red-shift Raman lines in SnSe (Gong et al. 2021, doi 10.1016/j.saa.2021.120375, reported this for SnSe single crystals). The fitted positions are not corrected for heating, and no laser-power series was taken. The thermal effect is small against the 30 to 60 cm-1 mismatch but is not zero.
